title: git: what it is for
summary: Every committed version of a project kept, with who changed what and why. Commits, branches and shared repositories, before any command.

scheme: which one? who changed what? why?
git: one folder, every committed version kept
text: git keeps the history of a folder: every version you commit, who made it and why.
- Code, configuration, documentation: any text that changes over time.
- You can go back to any version, compare two, and find the change that broke something.

scheme: each commit: a snapshot, its author,
its date, and a message saying why
text: A commit is a snapshot of the whole project, with who made it, when, and a message.
- Each commit points to the one before: the history is a chain.
- The message says why. Months later, it's the only place that answers "why is this line here?"

scheme: it works: merge it into main
text: A branch is a line of work beside the main one.
- Try an idea on it without touching what works.
- Ready: merge it back. A dead end: delete the branch, main never saw it.

scheme: ✘ a password, committed: in the history
for good, even if deleted later
text: Each person has the whole history; a shared repository is where the team meets.
- push sends your commits there; pull fetches the others' commits and merges them into yours.
- The history keeps everything: never commit a secret. If one gets in, change it: deleting it later doesn't remove it.
- Big binary files don't belong there either: every clone carries every version of them.
- The git lesson shows the commands, conflicts and undo.
